summary: In space, fire does not behave the way it does on Earth. Without gravity, flames turn spherical, ventilation decides whether they survive, and some materials burn with as little as 15% oxygen. To address this, we developed FIREFALL, a dashboard that unifies scattered NASA microgravity data to summarize, classify, and interpret fire behavior. Powered by validated machine learning models, it predicts whether a flame will survive or self-extinguish, while Astro, our AI assistant, explains the underlying physics in plain language. Because a fire on a spacecraft or lunar base leaves no escape route, understanding microgravity combustion is critical for choosing safer materials, ventilation systems, and detectors. Ultimately, our goal is to help engineers, students, and habitat designers anticipate and prevent fire risks before they happen.
details:
Overview & What It Does

FIREFALL transforms scattered data from NASA’s International Space Station fire experiments into an interactive, accessible simulation platform. By cleaning and structuring historical microgravity datasets, we trained machine learning models capable of predicting whether a flame will survive or extinguish under specific environmental conditions. Through our web interface, users can adjust gravity, oxygen concentration, and airflow in real time to watch how a flame reacts and ask Astro, our Mexican donkey astronaut AI assistant, to break down the science in plain language.

Impact & Vision

Fire behaves unpredictably in space, yet conducting physical combustion experiments off-Earth is extraordinarily expensive. FIREFALL centralizes fragmented NASA research into a single workspace where students, engineers, and mission designers can test scenarios and evaluate safer materials and ventilation strategies before investing in costly spaceflight trials. Built with bilingual support (English and Spanish) and an open, reproducible architecture, FIREFALL aims to democratize NASA fire science and scale alongside future experiments to support fire safety for upcoming missions to the Moon and Mars.

How We Built It

  • Data & Machine Learning: We sourced experimental records from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (BASS-I, BASS-II, FLEX, SAFFIRE-I, and ACME), the NASA Technical Reports Server, and NASA Science. Using Python, pandas, and NumPy, we engineered a unified variable combining gravity and airflow, allowing a single model to estimate flame behavior across the ISS, the Moon, and Mars. We trained and evaluated scikit-learn models (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting) and serialized the top performer using joblib.
  • Backend & AI Assistant: Built on FastAPI, our backend powers Astro using the Groq API (gpt-oss-120b) paired with a TF-IDF Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline grounded directly in NASA documentation.
  • Frontend & Visualization: Developed with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, featuring Chart.js for data analytics and HTML5 Canvas for real-time, model-driven flame animations.
  • Testing, Tooling & Deployment: Developed in Visual Studio Code, verified with pytest, version-controlled with Git/GitHub, and deployed across GitHub Pages, Docker, and Render. (Claude was used as a coding and documentation assistant, and Astro’s mascot artwork was AI-generated).

Engineering Considerations & Challenges

To ensure scientific integrity and reliability, we designed FIREFALL around several core constraints:

  • Data Quality & Imbalance: Because spaceflight fire datasets are scarce and heavily imbalanced, we selected our final model based on AUC rather than raw accuracy, and explicitly separated measured NASA data from model-estimated values in the interface.
  • Resilience & Security: We implemented graceful fallbacks so the interactive simulation remains fully functional even if the external AI server goes down, while strictly securing all API keys on the backend.
  • Accessibility & Compliance: We prioritized free, open-source tooling, full bilingual access, and strict adherence to NASA logo and media usage guidelines.
